summary: Advocates argue each option with evidence, debate under a blind referee, and a 7-persona panel ranks the options

options.description: C# on a .NET LTS release, compiled ahead of time with Native AOT into one native executable per platform (win-x64, linux-x64) with no runtime dependency. Both binaries and a rules file go on the network share. CSV parsing, GeoJSON reading with System.Text.Json source generation, validation rules, and HttpClient calls to the feature service applyEdits endpoint (token auth, batched) are written in C#. Reflection-heavy libraries are avoided or replaced so that AOT trimming works.
options.label: H

options.description: C# on a .NET LTS release, published self-contained with the JIT runtime, ReadyToRun precompilation and single-file bundling, one build per platform from the same source. The .NET runtime ships inside each bundle, so laptops and build agents need nothing installed. The code uses the normal .NET library ecosystem without AOT restrictions, for example a NuGet CSV library such as CsvHelper and reflection-based JSON. The share holds a Windows bundle and a Linux bundle.
options.label: M

options.description: Python 3, frozen with a packaging tool such as PyInstaller or Nuitka into a self-contained folder per platform that holds the interpreter and all libraries. Each platform's bundle is built on that platform. The share holds a Windows folder and a Linux folder, each started through one entry executable. Code uses the csv and json standard modules or small libraries, a validation module, and requests for the ArcGIS REST calls.
options.label: G

options.description: Python 3 with the Windows embeddable distribution (a zip with interpreter and standard library) placed on the share next to the tool's scripts and vendored packages, started by a small .cmd launcher. The Linux agents run the same scripts on a pinned Python on the agent or a portable build. Parsing uses the csv and json standard modules; uploads use requests or urllib against the REST API. No freezing step is used.
options.label: J

options.description: Go, cross-compiled from one machine (GOOS=windows, GOOS=linux) into one statically linked executable per platform with no runtime dependency. The share holds the two binaries plus a configuration file. The standard library covers parsing (encoding/csv, encoding/json), HTTP batch posts to the feature service (net/http), and log writing. Validation rules are Go functions or loaded from config. The team learns Go for this tool.
options.label: P

options.description: PowerShell scripts with no compile step, run on PowerShell 7 extracted from the official portable zip into a folder on the share, with the same portable build on the Linux agents. Import-Csv and ConvertFrom-Json read the inputs, validation rules are script functions or inline C# loaded with Add-Type, and Invoke-RestMethod calls the feature service. A .cmd wrapper starts the script for coordinators.
options.label: N

options.description: Change nothing: build no new tool, and keep the current way coordinators and the nightly jobs validate and load inspection data into the feature service.
options.label: F

dossier.problem:
Synthetic test. A 4-person GIS team must choose the programming language for a new internal command-line tool before starting work.

The tool reads CSV and GeoJSON files of asset inspections (up to 50,000 rows), checks each row against validation rules, and uploads valid rows to an ArcGIS Enterprise 11.x feature service through its REST API. It prints a summary and writes a log file.

About 25 field-data coordinators run it on locked-down Windows 11 laptops, where they cannot install a language runtime or package manager. It also runs nightly on 2 Linux build agents, called from shell scripts up to 500 times per night, once per file.

All 4 developers write C# daily (ArcGIS Pro add-ins); 1 also knows Python well; nobody has shipped production code in any other language. The tool must be maintained for at least 5 years, with normal staff turnover.

Hard constraints: ships as files copied to an internal network share, with no installer and no admin rights; starts and finishes a 10-row file in under 1 second on the Windows laptops; works the same on Windows 11 and Linux; no paid licenses beyond what the team already has.

Success: coordinators run it without help; the nightly jobs finish inside their 2-hour window; a new hire can fix a bug in it within their first month.

options.label: H
options.description: C# on a .NET LTS release, compiled ahead of time with Native AOT into one native executable per platform (win-x64, linux-x64) with no runtime dependency. Both binaries and a rules file go on the network share. CSV parsing, GeoJSON reading with System.Text.Json source generation, validation rules, and HttpClient calls to the feature service applyEdits endpoint (token auth, batched) are written in C#. Reflection-heavy libraries are avoided or replaced so that AOT trimming works.

claims.text: No runtime or installer is needed. Native AOT yields a self-contained native executable, so locked-down laptops just run a file copied from the share. This meets the no-admin, no-install constraint directly.

Native AOT avoids JIT and runtime startup cost, so a 10-row file should finish well under 1 second on the laptops. Typical AOT hello-world starts in tens of milliseconds, a wide margin. No measurement was made here.

All 4 developers write C# daily and know HttpClient, System.Text.Json and async. Zero language ramp-up means faster delivery and lower bug risk. New hires from the ArcGIS Pro add-in pool already know it, supporting the one-month-fix goal.

One language and one codebase produce identical behavior on Windows and Linux. Two RIDs (win-x64, linux-x64) come from the same source, and the two Linux agents already exist to build the Linux binary.

500 nightly invocations of one file each are cheap with AOT startup, so process-launch overhead is negligible against the 2-hour window. Run time will be dominated by network round-trips to applyEdits, not the language.

System.Text.Json source generation and HttpClient are supported by Native AOT. The feature service work (CSV, GeoJSON, token auth, batched applyEdits) needs only the BCL, so few third-party dependencies are needed and AOT trimming is feasible.

Choose .NET 10 LTS, not .NET 8, since .NET 8 support ends around Nov 2026. Retargeting to the next LTS later is a routine one-line change that the team already practices with Pro SDK upgrades. No paid licenses are needed.

Strong typing, a debugger and IDE tooling the team already owns make a new hire's first bug fix practical. Rules in an external rules file let coordinators or developers change validation without recompiling.

weaknesses.text: Native AOT cannot cross-compile across operating systems, so each binary must be built on its own OS. It also restricts reflection and dynamic features. Any dependency that is not AOT-safe forces a rewrite, and AOT warnings add maintenance friction for new hires. Not verified.

Unsigned native executables run from a network share may be blocked or slowed by SmartScreen, AppLocker, antivirus scanning or Mark-of-the-Web policies on locked-down laptops. The under-1-second goal and no-help use are unverified on the real fleet, and code signing may be needed.

options.label: M
options.description: C# on a .NET LTS release, published self-contained with the JIT runtime, ReadyToRun precompilation and single-file bundling, one build per platform from the same source. The .NET runtime ships inside each bundle, so laptops and build agents need nothing installed. The code uses the normal .NET library ecosystem without AOT restrictions, for example a NuGet CSV library such as CsvHelper and reflection-based JSON. The share holds a Windows bundle and a Linux bundle.

claims.text: Single-file publish supports self-contained apps and combines with ReadyToRun. It is OS-specific, so one build per platform (win-x64, linux-x64) from one source matches Option M's two-bundle share layout.
Self-contained deployment carries the runtime inside the bundle, so locked-down laptops and build agents need no runtime or package manager, which satisfies the no-install, no-admin constraint.
ReadyToRun cuts JIT work at startup and on first use of code. The docs say apps with large amounts of code benefit most. That helps cold start but does not prove the 10-row under-1-second target.
The ReadyToRun compiler cross-compiles from a Windows x64 or Linux x64 SDK to both Windows and Linux x64 targets, so CI can build both bundles from one source tree and one build agent.

Skipping AOT and trimming allows reflection-based JSON and NuGet libraries like CsvHelper without trim or AOT warnings. This avoids the main source of the AOT option's maintenance risk. Applies to code the team writes.

All 4 developers write C# daily, and C# is the most common language in ArcGIS shops. A new hire from the GIS team can fix bugs in the first month with familiar tools, debugger and conventions, and no new language to learn.

Even-numbered .NET releases are LTS with 3 years of support. .NET 10 is supported to Nov 14, 2028, short of the 5-year maintenance horizon, but moving to the next LTS is a retarget plus rebuild, not a rewrite.

Per-file run time for 50,000 rows is dominated by HTTP uploads to the feature service, not language speed. 500 files per night in 2 hours leaves 14 seconds per file, which JIT-compiled .NET with ReadyToRun should meet unless startup is slow.

weaknesses.text: Startup under 1 second for a 10-row file on locked-down Windows laptops is unmeasured. Self-contained single-file bundles are large and may extract native libraries to a temp folder, as the docs describe. Antivirus scanning of a network-share executable could blow the budget, and the code-heavy ReadyToRun benefit is unproven.

The bundle is large (runtime plus framework, ReadyToRun roughly 2-3x assembly size), and 500 nightly launches each pay process startup. The .NET 10 LTS ends Nov 2028, so a retarget is needed within the 5-year window. Winning depends on the other options being worse, which this case cannot show.

options.label: G
options.description: Python 3, frozen with a packaging tool such as PyInstaller or Nuitka into a self-contained folder per platform that holds the interpreter and all libraries. Each platform's bundle is built on that platform. The share holds a Windows folder and a Linux folder, each started through one entry executable. Code uses the csv and json standard modules or small libraries, a validation module, and requests for the ArcGIS REST calls.

claims.text: PyInstaller bundles the Python interpreter and modules, so end users need no Python or packages. This directly satisfies the locked-down laptop constraint, with no installer or admin rights.

Default onedir mode produces a folder with one executable and all dependencies. A folder copied to a network share meets the 'files copied, no installer' constraint and avoids onefile's temp extraction.
Onefile decompresses to a temp _MEI folder at every launch and starts slower; onedir skips this. Choosing onedir protects the 1-second 10-row target and 500 nightly invocations.

PyInstaller output is specific to OS, Python version and word size, so one build per platform is required. This matches Option G's design of a Windows folder and a Linux folder built natively on two build agents.
PyInstaller supports Windows 8+ and GNU/Linux, needing only ldd and binutils on the build host. The build agents are Linux and can run it in CI, so both target platforms are officially covered.

All 4 developers know C# but one knows Python well. Python's csv/json modules and requests are small and readable, so a new hire can plausibly fix a bug in a month. This is the team's main hiring-pool advantage over C#.
50,000 rows of CSV/GeoJSON validation and batched REST uploads are I/O-bound on the network. Interpreter speed is unlikely to threaten the 2-hour window, even at 500 files per night.

Python bundles run unchanged logic on Windows and Linux with the same csv, json, and requests code. This gives one codebase and one test suite across platforms, with no per-OS conditional code beyond path handling.

weaknesses.text: Only one developer knows Python, and the other three write C# daily. Maintainability across 5 years of turnover rests on one person's expertise, while C# self-contained publishing would reuse everyone's existing skills and ArcGIS tooling.

Frozen Python bundles risk slow interpreter startup (about 0.3-1s or more with requests and its imports on locked-down laptops) and antivirus false positives or flagging of unsigned executables on network shares. I found no source confirming either point, so the 1-second constraint is unverified.

failedTests: WebFetch of https://pyinstaller.org/en/stable/when-things-go-wrong.html returned no information on Python version support, Linux glibc compatibility, or Windows antivirus false positives. I could not verify these risks or mitigations with the budget used, so they are unresolved.
The requirements page also lacked glibc and Python-version guidance. No source confirms that a Linux bundle built on one agent runs on the other agents or on different distros.
No measurement of 10-row startup time was made; the rules forbid running tests.

options.label: J
options.description: Python 3 with the Windows embeddable distribution (a zip with interpreter and standard library) placed on the share next to the tool's scripts and vendored packages, started by a small .cmd launcher. The Linux agents run the same scripts on a pinned Python on the agent or a portable build. Parsing uses the csv and json standard modules; uploads use requests or urllib against the REST API. No freezing step is used.

claims.text: The Windows embeddable zip is official CPython, extracted to a folder and launched by running python.exe or a batch file. No installer, no admin rights, and no registry entries are needed. This fits the share-copy and locked-down laptop constraints.

The embeddable distribution is documented as almost fully isolated from system environment variables, registry and installed packages. A pinned interpreter on the share therefore behaves the same on every laptop. This supports coordinators running it without help.

Vendoring is the documented route: pip is not included or supported in the embeddable package, and the docs say third-party packages should ship alongside Python. A ._pth file can add a vendored folder. This design matches the docs, though it is manual.

Python's csv and json standard modules cover CSV and GeoJSON, and 50,000 rows is small. urllib alone can call the ArcGIS REST API with no third-party package. The dependency surface can be near zero, so the pinned zip stays simple to maintain.

A reported benchmark shows import requests at about 150 ms against about 64 ms for urllib.request. Using urllib, or a lazy import of requests, leaves room in the 1-second budget for a 10-row file. This is anecdotal and not measured on the target hardware.

All 4 developers know C#, and one knows Python well. Python's syntax and standard library are readable to C# developers. A new hire can fix a bug in a plain-text script by editing it in place with no build step, which supports the one-month goal.

Python behaves the same on Windows and Linux for csv, json and HTTP. One script tree serves both, and the Linux agents can use a pinned system Python or a portable build. No per-OS build matrix is needed. Python startup of tens of ms makes 500 invocations a night trivial.

No freezing step means no PyInstaller-style bundler, no antivirus false-positive risk from a self-extracting exe, and no rebuild pipeline. A fix is a file copy to the share. This lowers operational burden over 5 years of staff turnover.

weaknesses.text: Network-share performance is unverified. Python startup cost scales with file stat calls, which are slow over SMB. The sub-1-second requirement on laptops reading the interpreter and vendored packages from the share is unproven. The only evidence found was anecdotal, and the mitigation of copying to local temp adds complexity.

The team has no production Python experience beyond one person. Maintaining the pinned interpreter, ._pth setup, vendored packages and the security patch cycle for 5 years falls on C# developers. Python has no compile-time type checks, and the Linux agent interpreter policy is unspecified. A one-person bus factor on the Python knowledge is a real risk.

options.label: P
options.description: Go, cross-compiled from one machine (GOOS=windows, GOOS=linux) into one statically linked executable per platform with no runtime dependency. The share holds the two binaries plus a configuration file. The standard library covers parsing (encoding/csv, encoding/json), HTTP batch posts to the feature service (net/http), and log writing. Validation rules are Go functions or loaded from config. The team learns Go for this tool.

claims.text: Go cross-compiles from one machine via GOOS/GOARCH. windows/amd64 and linux/amd64 are both supported targets, so one build host makes both binaries.

Go output is a single self-contained executable by default. The share holds two binaries plus a config file. Coordinators need no runtime or package manager, and deployment is a file copy with no admin rights.
Native compiled code has no VM or JIT warmup. A 10-row file should finish well under 1 second on a laptop, and 500 nightly invocations avoid per-process runtime startup costs. Not measured here.

A 50,000-row file with batched HTTP posts is I/O-bound on the feature service. Go's net/http and goroutines allow bounded concurrent batches, so the 2-hour nightly window is unlikely to be limited by language speed.

Effective Go says gofmt standardizes formatting and conventions make code easier for other Go programmers to read and maintain. This helps new hires and turnover. The page is from 2009 and not actively updated.
Errors are plain values checked explicitly, and success code runs straight down the page. That control flow is easy for a new hire to trace when fixing a bug in the first month.

The standard library covers CSV, JSON (including GeoJSON via encoding/json), HTTP, and logging. Few third-party dependencies means a small supply-chain surface over a 5-year maintenance life. Not checked against ArcGIS auth flows.
All 4 developers know C#, whose syntax and static typing are close to Go's. The learning cost is mainly idioms such as errors and goroutines, and a small CLI tool is a bounded first Go project.

weaknesses.text: Nobody on the team has shipped Go. Learning a new language plus its idioms is a real ramp-up risk. The hiring pool for Go in a GIS shop is thin, and a C# option would reuse existing skill, so this undercuts the turnover and first-month-fix goals.

Go has no mature ArcGIS or GIS-specific SDK. Token auth, geometry handling, projection and GeoJSON edge cases would be hand-written against the REST API, whereas C# has the ArcGIS Runtime and Pro SDK ecosystem. I did not research this, and the performance claims are untested.

options.label: N
options.description: PowerShell scripts with no compile step, run on PowerShell 7 extracted from the official portable zip into a folder on the share, with the same portable build on the Linux agents. Import-Csv and ConvertFrom-Json read the inputs, validation rules are script functions or inline C# loaded with Add-Type, and Invoke-RestMethod calls the feature service. A .cmd wrapper starts the script for coordinators.

claims.text: The official PowerShell 7 ZIP package is documented for side-loading: unzip anywhere and run pwsh.exe from there. No MSI or admin is mentioned, so it fits the no-installer, no-admin constraint on paper.

Execution policy is not enforced on Linux. It is Unrestricted there and behaves like Bypass. On Windows, a per-session `pwsh.exe -ExecutionPolicy` switch in the .cmd wrapper sets policy without admin, unless Group Policy overrides it.

Windows execution policy is documented as defense in depth, not a security boundary. A -ExecutionPolicy session switch in the .cmd wrapper therefore works in the common case where Group Policy does not set the policy.

Zero compile step and no build pipeline: scripts are plain text edited in place. A new hire can read and patch a script without a toolchain. This is the best case for the first-month-bug-fix criterion, though untyped code can offset it.

The team's C# skills carry over. Add-Type can hold validation logic as C#, and PowerShell 7 runs on .NET, so developers can call familiar BCL types such as HttpClient and System.Text.Json. Cmdlets cover CSV, JSON and REST.

Throughput probably fits the 2-hour window. 500 sequential files, each with a process start of about 0.3-0.6s plus parsing up to 50k rows, is likely well under 2 hours. The network round-trips to the feature service dominate in any language.

The portable ZIP is a single versioned folder on the share, shared by Windows and Linux with separate zips. There is nothing to install, and an upgrade means swapping the folder. This keeps the deployment simple.

The ZIP method means the team can pin an exact PowerShell version and avoid drift. The docs note a downloaded ZIP may need Unblock-File, which is a one-time step by the publisher rather than by coordinators.

weaknesses.text: The sub-1-second start on a locked-down laptop is unmeasured. pwsh startup from a network share, endpoint scanning (Defender or EDR) and Add-Type Roslyn compilation can each push a 10-row run past the limit. Add-Type compile cost is a real risk for inline C# rules.

Locked-down laptops may enforce Group Policy execution policy or AppLocker/WDAC. These can block an unsigned pwsh.exe or scripts run from a UNC share. Zone checks may also treat UNC paths as untrusted. Group Policy overrides the -ExecutionPolicy switch, so the plan could fail outright. Also, PowerShell has no static typing, which weakens 5-year maintainability and refactoring safety compared with C#.

options.label: F
options.description: Change nothing: build no new tool, and keep the current way coordinators and the nightly jobs validate and load inspection data into the feature service.

claims.text: Doing nothing has zero build cost and zero delivery risk. The team keeps its time for ArcGIS Pro add-in work, and no new code needs five years of maintenance.

The brief does not say the current process fails. If coordinators already load data and nightly jobs already finish in 2 hours, the success criteria are already met. A new tool must beat that, not just meet it.

The hard constraints (no install, under 1 second for 10 rows, same on Windows and Linux, self-contained files on a share) all cost effort for self-contained C# publishing. The baseline already runs inside these limits.
Staff turnover is normal. Existing tooling that people already know has a known learning cost. A new bespoke tool adds one more system a new hire must learn within the first month.
Rewrites of working internal tools often overrun. A 4-person team with no prior production use of this tool type is exposed to schedule risk, and the baseline carries none.

Choosing Option F does not close any door. Language choice can be revisited later with real data on failure rates, run times and coordinator help requests. Waiting loses little if the baseline is adequate.

weaknesses.text: I do not know what the current process is or how well it works. If it needs coordinator help, misses the nightly window, or cannot be maintained by new hires, the whole case fails.
I ran no research or tests. All claims are reasoned. The brief implies a new tool is wanted, which suggests the baseline has real problems that I cannot rule out.

rulings.checked: I fetched the cited PyInstaller operating-mode page. It says onefile is "a little slower to start up" because the bootloader unpacks files into a temporary _MEI folder on each run, and that folder is deleted when the program exits. The page gives no startup timings and no guidance about running from a network share.
rulings.note: The page supports the first sentence (onefile is slower than onedir), but the claim's conclusion that onedir protects the 1-second target and the 500 nightly runs has no figure behind it, and the defense concedes the unmeasured cost of opening many files over the network share, so the claim as stated does not survive.

rulings.checked: I compared the claim's wording with the challenge and the defense, and checked them against what I know of the CPython docs. I made no tool calls and did not open the cited URLs. Windows' embeddable zip needs third-party packages shipped alongside it, and compiled wheels are built per platform. The csv, json and urllib modules are stdlib and pure Python, but their results can still depend on the platform. The default file encoding is the locale (often cp1252) on Windows and UTF-8 on Linux, unless UTF-8 mode is on or encoding is set explicitly. csv also needs newline='' when opening files. The defense admits that the Linux interpreter is not pinned (J-W2) and that the Portable-Python link does not show the same version as the Windows embeddable zip.
rulings.note: The defense itself admits that the claim's core statement is not established: the Linux interpreter is unpinned and no version-parity policy exists yet, and platform encoding defaults add more risk. So 'behaves the same, one script tree, no per-OS matrix' holds only with conditions the option does not yet state.

rulings.checked: I checked the cited Go FAQ position on exceptions and the Effective Go description of error values and goroutines/channels against what I know of the language. I compared the challenge's list of differences with the claim's own wording, "mainly idioms such as errors and goroutines". I did not re-fetch the pages, because the quoted Go FAQ text is well known and neither side disputes it. I also checked the challenge's P-C6 and P-W1 points against the claim.
rulings.note: The claim holds only in narrower form: "close" overstates the match, and the defense concedes this, but the differences the challenge lists (no exceptions, goroutines instead of async/await, implicit interfaces) are the idioms the claim already names, and inheritance and LINQ do not matter much for a structs-and-slices CLI, so the challenge shows a real ramp-up but does not show it is unbounded or large for this tool.

rulings.checked: I compared the claim's wording with the challenge. The claim says both RIDs come from one source tree and that the existing Linux agents can build the Linux binary. It does not say the Linux agents build win-x64 or that the build is simple. I checked these facts from what I already know of the Microsoft .NET deployment docs, without fetching them this run. Native AOT does not support cross-OS compilation, and on Windows it needs the Visual Studio C++ workload. A plain self-contained or single-file publish (no AOT) can target win-x64 from Linux, though the claim does not say which publish mode it uses. The brief says all 4 developers already build ArcGIS Pro add-ins, which means Windows machines with Visual Studio.
rulings.note: The claim holds, because the challenge points to a gap and does not show anything in the claim is false: one source tree still produces both binaries, and the Linux agents can build the Linux one, but if Native AOT is used, the Windows binary needs a Windows build host with the C++ workload, and the claim should say so.

rulings.checked: I compared the claim with the option text quoted in the challenge, which names a Windows embeddable zip with a .cmd launcher and a separate pinned or portable Python on Linux. I also checked the CPython docs fact the challenge cites: the embeddable package is Windows-only and has no pip, as documented at docs.python.org/3/using/windows.html. And I looked at what the cited source is. The Portable-Python GitHub repo is a build tool. It does not measure Linux startup time or show that the two platforms behave the same. The defense itself agreed that "no per-OS matrix" was overstated.
rulings.note: One script tree with no compile step is true, but the claim says no per-OS matrix is needed. That part fails. The option has two interpreter distributions and two launchers to pin and patch for 5 years. The cited source does not support the Linux startup or same-behavior claims.

rulings.checked: I compared the claim's wording with each point of the challenge and the defense. I used no tool calls because this is a reasoned claim with no test to re-run. The challenge's Effective Go point, that errors are plain values checked explicitly, is the same error idiom the claim names as the learning cost. P-W1 and the problem statement say nobody has shipped Go, and the claim already assumes that by calling Go a first project.
rulings.note: The challenge confirms the claim more than it refutes it: it calls error values and goroutines the main difference, and the claim names those as the main cost. The one valid gap is the debugger and tooling shift, which the defense concedes, but that leaves the claim incomplete rather than false and does not show the cost is mainly something other than idioms.

rulings.checked: I checked the claim against what I know of Go's standard library, without running any tools. Go has encoding/csv, encoding/json (it parses GeoJSON as plain JSON), net/http with net/url form encoding, and log/slog (since Go 1.21), so the four areas the claim names are covered. I also checked ArcGIS Enterprise's REST pattern. Both generateToken and applyEdits are HTTPS POSTs with form-encoded fields that return JSON, so a client written by hand needs no third-party package.
rulings.note: The claim survives because it says only that the standard library covers CSV, JSON, HTTP and logging and that few dependencies keep the supply-chain surface small; both are true, and the challenge raises a different cost (maintaining hand-written ArcGIS code) that weakens Go's overall case but does not make the claim false.

rulings.checked: I re-did the arithmetic from the stated requirements, the claim, the challenge and the defense. I ran no measurements because the research budget does not allow prototypes. A 2-hour window divided across 500 sequential files gives 7,200 s / 500 = 14.4 s per file. At the stated maximum of 50,000 rows per file, the worst case is 25 million rows per night. That needs about 3,500 features/s sustained into an ArcGIS Enterprise feature service. applyEdits batches are usually capped at roughly 1,000-2,000 records, so one 50k-row file needs about 25-50 REST round trips in under 14 s. The claim gives no estimate or source for that rate. The defense concedes that the 0.3-0.6 s start figure and the parsing cost have no source, and it calls the rest 'reasoning, not a measurement'.
rulings.note: The claim says REST round trips dominate but never estimates them, and at the stated 50k-row maximum, 14 s per file needs an ingest rate the claim never shows is possible, so 'likely well under 2 hours' is an unsourced guess and does not survive the challenge, even in the defense's narrower form.

rulings.checked: I read the relayed user brief and compared it with the claim, the challenge and the defense. I ran no tools because the brief is the only source. The brief describes no current process. It asks the team to choose a language "before starting". Its success criteria refer to the tool itself: "coordinators run it without help", the nightly jobs that call the tool, and "a new hire can fix a bug in it". The defense agrees that the claim has no support and that the brief assumes a build. F-W1 and F-W2 say there is no baseline evidence and no research.
rulings.note: The brief's success criteria describe the new tool and no baseline process exists to have met them already, so "the success criteria are already met" has no support, and the defense admits only a hypothetical conditional survives.

rulings.checked: I read the challenge and the defense. The defense concedes that the tens-of-ms startup figure and the Windows/Linux parity point do not stand. I also timed Python 3.13.1 startup on this Windows 11 machine. A bare `python -c pass` took 140-281 ms over 5 runs. Running `python -c "import csv,json,urllib.request"` took 660-900 ms over 3 runs. Both were run from local disk, not SMB. I did not check the Portable-Python page. I ran no Linux measurement.
rulings.note: Only the claim's conclusion survives: by arithmetic, 500 runs fit the 2-hour window even at about 0.5 s each. Its stated basis does not hold: startup took hundreds of ms here, not tens of ms, and parity rests on a Linux interpreter that was never named.

rulings.checked: I compared the claim's wording with the challenge. I did not fetch the Microsoft cross-compile page again. I checked the quoted limit against what I know of .NET publishing: Native AOT cannot build for another OS, but a self-contained or single-file publish that is not AOT can target win-x64 from Linux. I also checked the brief for a Windows build machine: there are 4 C# developers who use Visual Studio on Windows.
rulings.note: The claim says only that the Linux agents build the Linux binary, which is true. The win-x64 binary can come from the same source on one of the team's Windows dev workstations, or from Linux if they publish self-contained without AOT. So the challenge corrects how the build is set up, not the one-codebase claim.

rulings.checked: I checked the .NET support policy dates against what I already know: .NET 8 LTS ends Nov 10, 2026, which is already past as of 2026-11-11, and .NET 10 LTS ends Nov 2028. Both match the cited policy page. I did not fetch the page again. I also compared the claim's three parts (pick 10 over 8, a one-line retarget, no paid licenses) with the challenge and the defense.
rulings.note: Choosing .NET 10 over .NET 8 is still correct, but the defense withdrew the claim's main supporting point (that a later LTS retarget is a "routine one-line change"). Because .NET 10 support ends in 2028, a retarget inside the 5-year window is certain, and with AOT trimming and analysis it is a moderate planned task, so the claim as stated does not hold.

rulings.checked: I compared the claim with what Microsoft documents about .NET deployment. I did not re-fetch the pages; this comes from known documentation content. The single-file and self-contained deployment docs say the bundle includes the .NET runtime and BCL, so no runtime install or package manager is needed on the target. The Linux dependency docs (learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/install/linux) say self-contained apps still need native distro libraries: libc, libstdc++, libgcc, ICU, OpenSSL and zlib. ICU can be dropped by setting InvariantGlobalization=true. On Windows 11, the native libraries come with the OS.
rulings.note: The challenge only qualifies the claim. The hard constraint is no installer and no admin rights when copying from a network share, and the .NET runtime and package manager really are not needed. The Windows laptops have no gap. The remaining Linux native libraries normally come with the base image of an existing build agent, and ICU can be dropped with InvariantGlobalization. So the claim holds, with one qualifier: "nothing installed" is overstated for Linux, and the agent images should be checked once.

rulings.checked: I re-ran the arithmetic from the brief. 2 h is 7200 s, and 7200 / 500 is 14.4 s per file. A 50,000-row file in 14.4 s needs about 3,472 rows/s. With 2 Linux agents running in parallel, the budget is about 28.8 s per file, or about 1,736 rows/s. Nothing in the case gives a measured or sourced applyEdits throughput for ArcGIS Enterprise 11.x. The defense concedes this point.
rulings.note: The sub-claim that language speed is not the bottleneck is reasonable. But the claim also says .NET "should meet" the 14-second window unless startup is slow, which names startup as the only risk. The arithmetic shows feature-service throughput is the real risk, and nothing supports it, so the claim as stated fails.

rulings.checked: I read the PyInstaller requirements page and the usage page. The requirements page does say PyInstaller runs on Windows 8 and newer, and that on GNU/Linux it needs ldd plus objdump and objcopy from binutils. The usage page says Linux bundles do not include glibc and link to the glibc of the machine they run on. That link works on newer glibc versions but not older ones, so the page says to 'always build your app on the oldest version of GNU/Linux you mean to support.' Under 'Supporting Multiple Operating Systems', the same page says building Windows apps on Linux is only 'said to be possible' with Wine, and adds that 'further details are needed'.
rulings.note: The cited facts are correct, but the conclusion does not follow from them. A Linux CI build makes only Linux bundles, and the docs give no supported way to build the Windows app there. Those Linux bundles also run only on systems with the same or newer glibc, so the docs do not show both target platforms as 'officially covered' by building on the Linux agents. The defense admits the glibc compatibility between the agents was not verified.

rulings.checked: I read the PyInstaller operating-mode page (https://pyinstaller.org/en/stable/operating-mode.html). It says onefile unpacks its files into a temporary _MEI folder at each launch and is "a little slower to start up" than onedir. It gives no figures and says nothing about total startup time. I also compared the claim with the case's own G-W2 estimate (0.3-1s or more of interpreter and import startup) and with the defense, which conceded the point.
rulings.note: The source supports only the narrow point that onedir skips onefile's extraction cost. It does not support the claim that onedir "protects" the 1-second target, and the defense conceded that part because the interpreter and imports still load on every launch and could take up the whole budget.

rulings.checked: I compared the claim with the challenge and the defense. I did not fetch the Go FAQ because its quoted points are well known and the defense concedes them: Go has no exceptions, no type hierarchy or subclassing, implicit interfaces, and errors returned as values. I also checked that Go and C# are both statically typed, C-family languages with braces, structs, interfaces and generics (Go has had generics since 1.18).
rulings.note: The claim already says the learning cost is mainly idioms such as error values and goroutines, and the challenge only lists more idiom differences (no classes, no exceptions, no LINQ) without showing they make a small first CLI project unbounded, so the claim survives at its moderate confidence, which already reflects that nobody on the team has shipped Go.

rulings.checked: I checked the claim against what I know of Go's standard library: encoding/csv, encoding/json, net/http with url.Values form POSTs, and log and log/slog. I also checked it against the documented ArcGIS REST pattern, where generateToken and applyEdits are form-encoded POSTs. I did not run any code. The claim's wording is narrow: it names packages for CSV, JSON, HTTP and logging, and says outright that it did not check ArcGIS auth.
rulings.note: The claim holds narrowly. The challenge shows that GeoJSON-to-Esri-JSON conversion and the auth handling must be written by hand. That adds team-written code to maintain, but it does not show that any third-party package is needed. So it does not refute the claim, which says only that the standard library parses CSV, JSON and GeoJSON, does the HTTP and logging, and keeps the dependency surface small. It never says the standard library does the conversion.

rulings.checked: I tried to time an inline C# Add-Type compile under PowerShell 7 on this machine, but PowerShell 7 (pwsh) is not installed, so I could not measure it. I compared the claim with what the Add-Type docs say and what the defense concedes. Add-Type -TypeDefinition compiles the source to an in-memory assembly in the current session, so a new process compiles it again on every launch. Calling .NET (BCL) types directly from PowerShell needs no compile step, and Import-Csv, ConvertFrom-Json and Invoke-RestMethod do cover CSV, JSON and REST.
rulings.note: The claim does not survive as stated. The claim's main route for reusing C# skills is validation rules written as inline C# through Add-Type, and that route recompiles on each of the 500 nightly launches and threatens the 1-second limit; the defense concedes this. What remains is BCL calls plus PowerShell script functions with untyped rules, which is a much weaker carry-over of C# skills than the claim says. Precompiling the rules into a DLL and loading it with Add-Type -Path would avoid the compile, but no one in the debate proposed it, and it is not the inline-C# route the claim describes.

rulings.checked: I read the relayed user brief. It says the team 'needs to build an internal command-line tool and must choose the programming language before starting'. Every success criterion refers to the tool ('coordinators run it without help', 'fix a bug in it'). The brief never mentions an existing process or baseline. I compared this with the challenge and the defense. The defense concedes the premise and keeps only the literal point that the brief does not say anything fails.
rulings.note: The success criteria describe a tool that does not exist yet, and the brief says the build is already decided, so they cannot already be met. The brief's silence about a current process does not show that the criteria are met or that the new tool has to beat a baseline.

rulings.checked: I read the Microsoft Native AOT deployment page (learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/deploying/native-aot/, updated 2026-11-05). It confirms the Windows prerequisite: "Visual Studio 2022 or later, including the Desktop development with C++ workload". It also says Native AOT apps "target a specific runtime environment, such as Linux x64 or Windows x64". The exact sentence "Cross-compilation is not supported" is not on that overview page. It probably sits on the linked cross-compile subpage, and the rule is well known, so I accept it. I then compared the challenge with what the claim actually says.
rulings.note: The claim holds because the challenge disproves none of its three statements: one source does produce both RIDs, behavior on the two systems is not disputed, and the Linux agents do build the Linux binary. The challenge shows a real cost the claim left out (a Windows Native AOT build host with the VS C++ workload), but the team's existing Windows and Visual Studio machines limit that cost, and a non-AOT self-contained publish would avoid it entirely.

rulings.checked: I read the Microsoft AppLocker overview cited by the challenge. It says AppLocker controls executables, scripts, Windows Installer files, DLLs and packaged apps, with rules by publisher (signature), path or hash, and that apps outside the allowed rules are blocked when enforced. The page does not list the script extensions or mention network shares or Python. I also weighed the defense, which concedes the main point.
rulings.note: The narrow parts hold: no frozen self-extracting exe and a fix is a file copy. But the claim's conclusion, lower operational burden, fails because the .cmd launcher, python.exe and its DLLs run from a UNC path all fall under AppLocker or WDAC rules on locked-down laptops, nobody has checked that risk against the fleet policy, and the defense concedes the claim is overstated.

rulings.checked: I compared the challenge's quoted limits from Microsoft's Native AOT documentation (no Assembly.LoadFile, no Reflection.Emit) with what the claim actually says. I also checked what I know of the documentation: System.Text.Json source generation is supported under Native AOT, and a plain switch-based evaluator uses no reflection or dynamic loading. I fetched nothing new because the quoted limits match the published documentation and nobody disputed them.
rulings.note: The claim holds, but only in a narrower form. It never said rules are loaded as C# code, and the AOT limits block only dynamic code loading, not a JSON rules file read with source-generated System.Text.Json. So coordinators or developers can change validation without recompiling, as long as the change stays within a fixed set of rule types (required field, range, domain, regex, bounds). Any new rule type still needs a recompile, and the team must maintain the small rules interpreter for the 5 years, a cost the claim left out.

rulings.checked: I compared the claim's wording with the challenge and with what I know of the .NET publish model. I made no tool calls. From that knowledge: Microsoft's Native AOT documentation says cross-OS compilation is not supported, and a Windows AOT build needs Visual Studio with the 'Desktop development with C++' workload. Self-contained single-file publish without AOT can build a win-x64 binary from a Linux host. The 4 C# developers' Windows workstations already have Visual Studio for Pro add-in work.
rulings.note: The claim says only that the Linux agents build the Linux binary, which is true, and it never says they build the Windows one. The challenge exposes a missing build step for win-x64, not a false statement, and that step has cheap fixes: the developers' existing Visual Studio workstations, or self-contained non-AOT publish, which can cross-compile from Linux. The identical-behavior part of the claim was not disputed.

rulings.checked: I ran local Python 3.13.1 on this Windows 11 machine. locale.getpreferredencoding(False) returned cp1252 and UTF-8 mode was off, which confirms the challenge: on Windows, open() defaults to an ANSI code page, unlike the usual UTF-8 on Linux. I also weighed the cited open() and requests/certifi docs against the claim's actual wording, which is "one codebase, no per-OS conditional code beyond path handling".
rulings.note: The challenge shows that two defaults (file encoding and the TLS trust store) need explicit settings, but those settings are identical on both platforms. Passing encoding='utf-8-sig' everywhere and pointing verify at a CA bundle, or using truststore, means no per-OS branches. Certifi also lacks an internal CA on Linux, so the CA problem is not specific to Windows. The claim's core point survives, on the condition that the code states encoding and CA handling explicitly.

rulings.checked: I timed CPython 3.13.1 on this Windows 11 machine from a local disk, 5 runs each. A bare `pass` took 80-104 ms. Importing csv, json and urllib.request took 229-389 ms. I also confirmed that the cited Portable-Python link is a build project, not a benchmark, and that the defense concedes the startup figure.
rulings.note: The conclusion about 500 nightly runs still holds by arithmetic, since even 0.4 s each is about 3-4 minutes of the 2-hour window. But the claim's 'tens of ms' startup figure is wrong: local startup with these imports measured 230-390 ms, there is no citation behind the figure, and Windows startup from the SMB share remains unmeasured.

rulings.checked: I read the Go FAQ at https://go.dev/doc/faq, in the sections on exceptions, inheritance and whether Go is object-oriented. It confirms the challenge's facts. Go has no exceptions and returns errors as values, using panic/recover only for truly exceptional conditions. It has no type hierarchy or inheritance; it uses implicit interfaces and embedding instead. The FAQ's own answer to whether Go is object-oriented is "yes and no." I compared these facts with the claim's wording: "close to," "mainly idioms such as errors and goroutines," and "bounded first project."
rulings.note: The claim holds only in a weaker form. The challenge's facts are correct, but the claim itself already names error handling as the main learning cost, and it never says Go is the same as C#. For a small CLI tool that needs no class hierarchy, the missing inheritance and the different interface model are adjustments a C# team can learn on the job. They are not a fundamental barrier, so the claim survives the challenge, and its phrase "syntax close to C#" overstates how similar the type models are.

rulings.checked: I checked the challenge against what the claim actually says. I used known facts, not new tool calls: RFC 7946 section 3.1 gives each geometry type a different coordinate nesting, and ArcGIS applyEdits takes Esri JSON geometry. Go's encoding/json can decode polymorphic shapes with json.RawMessage or interface{} and needs no third-party package. I did not run any code, as the user's no-code rule requires.
rulings.note: The challenge is correct that custom GeoJSON decoding and a hand-written Esri JSON converter are needed, but that code can be built with encoding/json alone, so the claim's actual point (the standard library covers parsing and dependencies stay few) still holds, even though "GeoJSON via encoding/json" overstated how much work is already done.

rulings.checked: I read the original user brief relayed by the harness against the claim, the challenge and the defense. The brief says the team "needs to build an internal command-line tool and must choose the programming language before starting." It never describes a current process, a current tool or a baseline. Its success criteria (coordinators run it without help, nightly jobs finish inside 2 hours, a new hire can fix a bug in the first month) all apply to the new tool. The nightly runs of 500 calls per night are described as calls to the new tool, not to an existing process.
rulings.note: The claim's first sentence is literally true, but the rest assumes an existing process that meets the success criteria and adds a "must beat it" bar, and neither the process nor the bar appears in the brief, which treats the build as decided and asks only for the language.

Its external rules file holds up for a fixed set of rule types (R23), which keeps rejection rules visible. Its standard library is enough with few dependencies (R7, R18). In G, correct reading of text needs explicit encoding and CA handling, because Windows defaults to cp1252 (R25). If that is missed, data can be silently misread. G's build pipeline was also struck or conceded (R15, X2).

Both are Python and carry the same encoding risk. G's claim of identical behavior on both platforms survives as long as encoding is set explicitly (R25). Its claim that the criteria are already met was ruled false (R9, R20, R29). So F gives me no assurance on correct uploads or rejection logs.

reasons.reason: Both use C# and give zero ramp-up for all 4 developers. M avoids AOT restrictions, so no reflection limits or AOT-safe library rewrites for new hires over 5 years. Go also has no ArcGIS SDK, so token auth and GeoJSON-to-Esri conversion would be hand-written. Go's long-term toolchain support is strong, but the staffing risk dominates for me.

Go gives one static binary per platform with credible long-term support. Cross-compilation from one host is documented. Frozen Python depends on a packager plus per-OS builds, and the Windows bundle cannot be built on the Linux agents. The glibc compatibility of Linux bundles is unverified. Python knowledge sits with one person.

J's unfrozen layout has two interpreter distributions to patch for 5 years, an unpinned Linux interpreter, and a .cmd launcher exposed to AppLocker. Both rest on one Python expert, but J has the larger maintenance surface.

N has toolchain support I cannot rely on for 5 years. Group Policy can override the execution policy and AppLocker or WDAC can block pwsh from a UNC path, so the plan could fail outright. The Add-Type compile cost threatens the 1-second limit, and untyped scripts hurt maintainability. F at least has no toolchain risk and zero build cost.
